Vāyupurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The contribution of the पुराणस् to the growth of popular हिन्दुइस्म् is significant. Even the treatises and digests of धर्मशास्त्रस् have quoted profusely from them. One such purāṇa, classed among the 18 Mahāpurāṇas is the Vāyupurāṇa or Vāyavīyapurāṇa.
It has two khaṇḍas or sections. The Pūrvakhaṇḍa (first part) has 61 adhyāyas (chapters) and the Uttarakhaṇḍa (second part) has 50 adhyāyas. The total number of verses comes to about 12,000.
This purāṇa was first taught by the deity वायु to the sage वैशम्पायन. It was later narrated by the Sūtapaurāṇika, known as लोमहर्षण, to the sages शौनक and others who were engaged in the performance of a सत्त्रयाग in the नैमिषारण्य forest.
The contents of this purāṇa can be summarised as follows:
On च्रेअतिओन्; varṇas and āśramas; योग; description of प्रणव or ओङ्कार; lineages of sages; the four युगस्; some geographical details of जम्बूद्वीप (where भारतवर्ष or greater India is situated); various regions of the created world; churning of the milky ocean; manifestation of शिव as लिङ्ग; stories of वेदव्यास and his disciples; śrāddhas or obsequial rites, speciality of śrāddha done at गया; some sages and kings; greatness of Lord विष्णु and his incarnations; description of the fourteen worlds; greatness and importance of this purāṇa.
See also PURĀṆAS.

Vāyu
------------------------------------------
Vāyu or air is one of the पञ्चभूतस् or five basic elements of the world. वायु is also the presiding deity over it and is said to be dikpālaka (lord of the quarters) ruling in the direction of north-west.
Hanumān and भीम were born due to his grace.
Vāyu as vital air acts inside the body as five major prāṇas and five subsidiary prāṇas (upaprāṇas).
Iconographical works describe him as white or ash-grey in complexion. He has two hands carrying a bow and an arrow. He rides on a deer.
Some works describe him as having four arms holding a banner (dhvaja) with two and a water-pot in the third, the last hand showing varadamudrā (gesture of giving boons).
Sometimes the four hands are shown as holding पाश (noose), aṅkuśa (goad), kamala (lotus) and दण्ड (cudgel).
Vāyu’s palace is called Gandhavatī.
